title: Who are the barbarians?
hookLine: Montaigne asks whether the peoples of Brazil that Europeans call savage are more barbaric than Europe's own wars (Essays 1.31)

cards: A pair of trousers. That's where today's essay lands. To get there, Montaigne travels a long way without leaving home.
He starts with a man in his household who had lived a long time on the coast of Brazil, and who told him about the people there. He moves through what Europeans of his day said about those people.
And he ends up back in France, in the middle of its own wars, carrying one question the whole way: who are the barbarians?

teach.b: First, the turn. The essay is called Of Cannibals. From what he's been told, Montaigne says, he finds nothing barbarous or savage in these people, except that each of us calls barbarous whatever isn't our own custom.
Here the idea of custom gets teeth. Second, the mirror. He doesn't pretend the people he heard about were gentle.

He describes them killing enemies in war and eating them. There is more barbarity, he says, in eating a man alive than dead: in tearing apart by torture a body that can still feel, and roasting it bit by bit.
He says he has seen this done, not among old enemies but among neighbors and fellow citizens, under cover of piety and religion.
He was describing his own country, in his own time. Third, the visitors. Some of these men came to France, and Montaigne records what struck them.
They found it strange that so many tall, bearded, armed men would obey a child instead of choosing one of their own to lead.

And they'd noticed some people stuffed with every good thing while others, whom they called their halves, begged at their doors, thin with hunger. They wondered why the hungry put up with it. Fourth, the trousers.
The essay ends with a shrug in the reader's voice: not bad at all, but so what?
Montaigne lets his reader sneer, and the sneer gives the reader away. One honest note: he never went to Brazil. It all came secondhand, and he tells us whose hands.

how: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Cannibals as practice in turning a judgment around: before calling another people barbarous, look hard at what your own side does.

games.q: what does “who are the barbarians?” mean?
o: a history lesson about the tribes that invaded ancient Rome
a traveler's guide to the customs of the people of Brazil
a question that turns the label barbarous back on ourselves

s: Montaigne says the people he heard about never did anything harsh
he describes them killing and eating enemies taken in war, then says torturing the living is worse.
he points to cruelty done by neighbors and fellow citizens in his own time
he says he has seen it, and under cover of piety and religion.
Montaigne sailed to Brazil to see for himself
he never went; he relied on a man in his household who had lived there, and on other reports.

games.q: you're Montaigne. you've just written that the people of Brazil eat enemies killed in war. what comes next on the page?
o: a warning to readers about savages.
the cruelties you've seen neighbors do to each other in your own country's wars.
games.why: he turns the lens around: tearing apart a living body by torture, done among fellow citizens under cover of religion, is more barbarous than eating the dead.

practice: Bring to mind an ordinary group you tend to call them, not the worst you can think of: people who vote, raise kids or eat dinner another way.

Find one habit of theirs that looks odd to you, then turn it around the way Montaigne does: which habit of yours would look odd from their side of the table? Hold both for a while, without deciding who wins.

wordCard.voice: Who are the barbarians? Montaigne's question in Of Cannibals: each of us calls barbarous what isn't our own custom, and sometimes the cruelty is closer to home. Today's word.

orig.s: chacun appelle barbarie ce qui n'est pas de son usage
orig.say: shah-KUN ah-PELL bar-bah-REE suh kee nay pah duh sohn ew-ZAHZH
orig.note: French, Montaigne's own words in Of Cannibals: each person calls barbarism whatever isn't their own custom.

carryVoice: Your line: who are the barbarians. Montaigne's question turns the mirror around before it points. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Essays 1.31, Of Cannibals (each calls barbarous what is not his custom; more barbarity in eating a man alive than dead; torture among neighbors under cover of piety; the visitors' remarks on obeying a child and on their 'halves' begging; the ending about breeches)
